paragraphs: The number of members of which the House of Representatives is to consist offers another very interesting point of view from which to consider this branch of the federal legislature. Scarcely any article in the whole Constitution seems made more worthy of attention by the weight of character and the apparent force of argument with which it has been attacked. The charges brought against it are these. First, that so small a number of representatives will be an unsafe depositary of the public interests. Secondly, that they will not have a proper knowledge of the local circumstances of their numerous constituents. Thirdly, that they will be taken from the class of citizens that will sympathize least with the feelings of the mass of the people, and will be most likely to aim at a permanent elevation of the few on the depression of the many. Fourthly, that however defective the number will be at the outset, it will become more and more disproportionate as the people increase and as obstacles prevent a corresponding increase of the representatives.

In general it may be remarked on this subject that no political problem is less capable of a precise solution than that of the most convenient number for a representative legislature. Nor is there any point on which the policy of the individual States differs more, whether we compare their legislative assemblies directly with each other or consider the proportions they respectively bear to the number of their constituents. Set aside the difference between the smallest and largest States, such as Delaware, whose most numerous branch consists of twenty-one representatives, and Massachusetts, where it amounts to between three and four hundred. A very considerable difference can still be seen among States nearly equal in population. The number of representatives in Pennsylvania is not more than one fifth of that in the State last mentioned. New York, whose population is to that of South Carolina as six to five, has little more than one third of the number of representatives. As great a disparity prevails between the States of Georgia and Delaware or Rhode Island. In Pennsylvania the representatives do not bear a greater proportion to their constituents than one for every four or five thousand. In Rhode Island they bear a proportion of at least one for every thousand. And under the constitution of Georgia the proportion may be carried to one for every ten electors, and must unavoidably far exceed the proportion in any of the other States.

Another general remark is that the ratio between the representatives and the people ought not to be the same where the people are very numerous as where they are very few. Were the representatives in Virginia regulated by the standard in Rhode Island, they would at this time amount to between four and five hundred, and twenty or thirty years from now to a thousand. On the other hand, Pennsylvania's ratio, if applied to the State of Delaware, would reduce the latter's representative assembly to seven or eight members. Nothing can be more fallacious than to found our political calculations on arithmetical principles. Sixty or seventy men may more properly be trusted with a given degree of power than six or seven. But it does not follow that six or seven hundred would be proportionately a better depositary. And if we carry the supposition on to six or seven thousand, the whole reasoning ought to be reversed. The truth is that in all cases a certain number at least seems necessary to secure the benefits of free consultation and discussion and to guard against too easy a combination for improper purposes. On the other hand, the number ought at most to be kept within a certain limit, in order to avoid the confusion and intemperance of a multitude. In all very numerous assemblies, of whatever character composed, passion never fails to wrest the scepter from reason. Had every Athenian citizen been a Socrates, every Athenian assembly would still have been a mob.

It is also necessary to recall here the observations that were applied to the case of biennial elections. The limited powers of Congress and the control of the State legislatures justify less frequent elections than the public safety might otherwise require. For the same reason, the members of Congress need be less numerous than if they possessed the whole power of legislation and were under no restraints other than the ordinary ones on other legislative bodies.

With these general ideas in mind, let us weigh the objections that have been stated against the number of members proposed for the House of Representatives. It is said, in the first place, that so small a number cannot be safely trusted with so much power.

The number of which this branch of the legislature is to consist at the outset of the government will be sixty-five. Within three years a census is to be taken, when the number may be increased to one for every thirty thousand inhabitants; and within every successive period of ten years the census is to be renewed, and increases may continue to be made under the same limitation. It will not be thought an extravagant conjecture that the first census will, at the rate of one for every thirty thousand, raise the number of representatives to at least one hundred. Counting the negroes at three fifths, it can scarcely be doubted that the population of the United States will by that time, if it does not already, amount to three millions. At the end of twenty-five years, according to the computed rate of increase, the number of representatives will amount to two hundred, and at the end of fifty years to four hundred. This is a number that, I presume, will put an end to all fears arising from the smallness of the body. I take for granted here what I shall show hereafter, in answering the fourth objection, that the number of representatives will be increased from time to time in the manner the Constitution provides. On a contrary supposition, I should admit that the objection has very great weight indeed.

The true question to be decided, then, is whether the smallness of the number, as a temporary regulation, is dangerous to the public liberty. Is sixty-five members for a few years, and a hundred or two hundred for a few more, a safe depositary for a limited and well-guarded power of legislating for the United States? I must own that I could not give a negative answer to this question without first wiping out every impression I have received about the present character of the people of America, the spirit that actuates the State legislatures, and the principles incorporated into the political character of every class of citizens. I am unable to conceive that the people of America, in their present disposition or under any circumstances that can speedily arise, will choose, and every second year repeat the choice of, sixty-five or a hundred men who would be disposed to form and pursue a scheme of tyranny or treachery. I am unable to conceive that the State legislatures, which must feel so many motives to watch the federal legislature and possess so many means of counteracting it, would fail either to detect or to defeat a conspiracy by the latter against the liberties of their common constituents. I am equally unable to conceive that there are at this time, or can be in any short time, in the United States any sixty-five or a hundred men capable of recommending themselves to the choice of the people at large who would either desire or dare, within the short space of two years, to betray the solemn trust committed to them. What change of circumstances, time and a fuller population of our country may produce, requires a prophetic spirit to declare, and that makes no part of my pretensions. But judging from the circumstances now before us, and from their probable state within a moderate period of time, I must pronounce that the liberties of America cannot be unsafe in the number of hands proposed by the federal Constitution.

From what quarter can the danger come? Are we afraid of foreign gold? If foreign gold could so easily corrupt our federal rulers and enable them to ensnare and betray their constituents, how has it happened that we are at this time a free and independent nation? The Congress that conducted us through the Revolution was a less numerous body than their successors will be. They were not chosen by, nor responsible to, their fellow citizens at large. Though appointed from year to year and recallable at pleasure, they were generally continued for three years, and before the ratification of the federal articles for a still longer term. They always held their consultations under the veil of secrecy. They had the sole conduct of our affairs with foreign nations. Throughout the whole course of the war they had the fate of their country more in their hands than it is to be hoped will ever be the case with our future representatives. And from the greatness of the prize at stake, and the eagerness of the party that lost it, it may well be supposed that means other than force would not have been scrupled. Yet we know from happy experience that the public trust was not betrayed; nor has the purity of our public councils in this respect ever suffered, even from the whispers of slander.

Is the danger feared from the other branches of the federal government? But where are the means to be found by the President, or the Senate, or both? Their pay for office, it is to be presumed, will not, and without a prior corruption of the House of Representatives cannot, more than suffice for very different purposes. Their private fortunes, since they must all be American citizens, cannot possibly be sources of danger. The only means they can possess, then, will be in the dispensing of appointments. Is it here that suspicion rests her charge? Sometimes we are told that this fund of corruption is to be exhausted by the President in subduing the virtue of the Senate. Now it is the fidelity of the other House that is to be the victim. The improbability of such a mercenary and treacherous combination among the several members of the government, who stand on foundations as different as republican principles will well allow and are at the same time accountable to the society over which they are placed, ought alone to quiet this apprehension. But fortunately the Constitution has provided a still further safeguard. The members of Congress are made ineligible to any civil offices that may be created, or whose pay may be increased, during the term for which they were elected. No offices, therefore, can be dealt out to the existing members except those that may become vacant by ordinary casualties. To suppose that these would be enough to buy the guardians of the people, selected by the people themselves, is to renounce every rule by which events ought to be calculated, and to substitute an indiscriminate and unbounded jealousy against which all reasoning must be vain. The sincere friends of liberty who give themselves up to the extravagances of this passion are not aware of the injury they do their own cause. There is a degree of depravity in mankind that requires a certain degree of circumspection and distrust; but there are other qualities in human nature that justify a certain portion of esteem and confidence. Republican government presupposes the existence of these qualities in a higher degree than any other form. Were the pictures drawn by the political jealousy of some among us faithful likenesses of the human character, the inference would be that there is not sufficient virtue among men for self-government, and that nothing less than the chains of despotism can restrain them from destroying and devouring one another.
